analysis.one_liner: Sets the federal minimum wage locally, as a share of average pay adjusted for local living costs.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one House Republican with zero cosponsors, never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would replace the flat federal minimum wage with a floor set area by area: 40% of the national average hourly wage for private-sector nonsupervisory workers, raised or lowered for each metro area's or rural area's cost of living, phasing to 45% after one year and 50% after two. It would also raise the required cash wage for tipped employees to 30% of that regional minimum, up from the current $2.13, and raise the subminimum for newly hired teen workers to two-thirds of it. The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-wage workers, especially in higher-cost metropolitan areas where the regional formula would set the floor well above the current federal minimum. Tipped workers and newly hired teenagers would also see their required cash wages rise above today's levels, though by less.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the flat federal minimum wage with a wage set for each metropolitan area or nonmetropolitan portion, calculated as 40% of the national average hourly wage for private-sector nonsupervisory workers, multiplied by a cost-of-living adjustment factor ranging from 87.5% to 115% based on the area's regional price parity.
The wage percentage phases up to 45% of the national average after one year and 50% after two years, and the formula keeps the floor from ever falling in later years.
Raises the minimum cash wage employers must pay tipped employees to 30% of the regional minimum wage, replacing the current fixed low cash wage.
Raises the subminimum wage for newly hired workers 18 or younger (24 or younger in Puerto Rico) to two-thirds of the regional minimum wage, up from the current fixed $4.25.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retail, hospitality, and other low-wage businesses — would face higher payrolls, with the largest increases in high-cost metropolitan areas and the smallest in low-cost rural and small-town areas.
analysis.who_pays_short: Low-wage employers like restaurants and retail

drawbacks.text: The regional adjustment permanently locks in lower wage floors in low-cost areas — largely rural regions and small metros — so workers in those places would get much smaller raises than a flat national increase would give them, and geographic pay gaps would become federal policy.

The bill keeps the tip credit: restaurants could still pay servers as little as 30% of the regional minimum in cash and count tips toward the rest, and it keeps a subminimum wage of two-thirds of the regional minimum for newly hired teen workers.

The target — 50% of the national average wage — is a lower goal than the flat minimum wage increases proposed in the same Congress, so the raise would be smaller for many workers, particularly outside expensive coastal metros.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine but geographically uneven raise. In expensive metros it would push the floor well above today's federal minimum; in low-cost areas the increase would be modest, and the formula would make those lower floors permanent federal policy rather than a step toward convergence. Keeping the tip credit and the teen subminimum blunts the benefit for some of the lowest-paid workers. A supporter would argue the local formula protects small businesses and rural economies from a one-size-fits-all number; a critic would answer that a worker's rent may be lower in a small town but not by half, and the bill writes that gap into law.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Brian Fitzpatrick, a Republican, introduced the Fair Wage Act of 2019 on September 20, 2019, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
No member of either party cosponsored the bill — the cosponsor list was empty.
The action history shows only two entries: introduction and the committee referral. No markup, no vote, no further action of any kind followed.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died without ever leaving committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have paid the higher regional minimum wage are better off, particularly in low-cost areas where a flat national increase would have cost the most, along with the restaurant industry, which kept the existing low cash wage for tipped workers. Low-wage workers are where they started, with the federal minimum unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who avoided higher wage costs

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Wage Act of 2019 and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral for all minimum wage legislation in the House
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled it for consideration; no markup, vote, or report followed in the 15 months remaining in the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican introduced the bill and zero members of either party — not even fellow Republicans — cosponsored it, so no party bloc ever took a position; the Democratic-run committee simply never acted.

industries.note: The bill would raise the required cash wage for tipped employees from $2.13 to 30% of the regional minimum, a real cost — but it also permanently preserves the tip credit, letting restaurants count customer tips toward most of a server's wage. What the industry saves on wages is what tipped workers go without.

The bill would raise payroll costs for businesses that pay minimum wage, with the largest increases in high-cost metros and the smallest in low-cost rural areas — the regional formula is what keeps their costs down relative to a flat national increase.
The bill would raise the teen subminimum from a fixed $4.25 to two-thirds of the regional minimum wage for newly hired workers 18 and under, though it keeps the subminimum itself in place.
